prompt: A client uses full jitter: it waits a uniformly random time between zero and its capped exponential backoff. The backoff has reached its cap. What should happen on later retries?

options.text: Keep choosing a random delay within the capped interval.
options.explanation: Correct. The cap stops interval growth; the delay is still chosen randomly.

options.text: Every client waits exactly the cap.
options.explanation: That removes jitter and can synchronise clients again.

options.text: Ignore the cap and keep doubling indefinitely.
options.explanation: That defeats the configured maximum wait.

options.text: Retry immediately forever because the cap was reached.
options.explanation: Reaching a delay cap does not remove attempt, deadline or load budgets.

workedExample: Full jitter has two decisions: bound the retry interval, then sample a delay within it. Once the interval reaches its cap, the random sample still changes. A capped delay alone does not decide whether another retry is safe or affordable.

prompt: A mobile app, gateway and Orders service each retry calls to the next layer. During a Payments outage, why can this overload Payments even when each layer allows only a few attempts?

options.text: Only the outer layer can cause traffic.
options.explanation: Every outer attempt can trigger inner retries.

options.text: Retry counts simply add, so nesting has little effect.
options.explanation: Nested attempts can each run a full inner sequence.

options.text: Retries multiply across layers; choose a retry owner and enforce shared deadlines and budgets.
options.explanation: Correct. Per-layer limits do not by themselves bound the composed load tightly.
It protects intended effects within its contract, not request volume.

workedExample: One gateway retry can repeat all of the Orders service’s attempts. An app retry can repeat that entire sequence. Put retries at an appropriate layer with enough context, propagate deadlines and cap additional load.

prompt: A dependency is fully unavailable. Clients already use exponential backoff and have a per-request attempt limit. What does a fleet-wide retry budget add?

options.text: It guarantees every request eventually succeeds.
options.explanation: A budget bounds extra work; it cannot restore an unavailable service.

options.text: It caps aggregate extra retry traffic, even when many original requests fail together.
options.explanation: Correct. Delays and individual limits alone do not impose the same fleet-wide load bound.

options.text: It replaces the need for deadlines.
options.explanation: An operation can still outlive its useful deadline even within a traffic budget.

options.text: It makes non-idempotent operations safe to repeat.
options.explanation: Retry safety requires an appropriate operation or deduplication contract.

workedExample: Backoff spreads attempts over time. A per-request limit bounds one operation. A retry budget limits how much extra traffic the population may add, so an outage does not turn every original request into its full retry allowance.

prompt: A database blips and 10,000 clients get an error at the same instant. Each waits before retrying: policy A uses plain exponential backoff, so every client waits exactly 2 s; policy B uses full jitter, so each waits a uniformly random time between 0 and 2 s. What does the database see?

options.text: Both deliver 10,000 retries, so the load is the same
options.explanation: The *total* is the same, but the *peak* isn't. A database copes with a steady rate far better than with everything arriving in the same instant.

options.text: A: about 5,000/s for two seconds; B: all 10,000 exactly 2 s later
options.explanation: This is the right pair of outcomes attached to the wrong policies. The fixed wait is what synchronises clients.

options.text: B is worse, because some clients retry almost immediately
options.explanation: A few early retries are cheap. Spreading arrivals across the window is exactly what keeps the peak low.

options.text: A: all 10,000 retries arrive together 2 s after the blip; B: roughly 5,000/s spread across the 2 s window
options.explanation: Correct. Without jitter the clients stay in lockstep, a thundering herd on every retry round. Full jitter spreads 10,000 retries over 2 s, about 5 per millisecond.

workedExample: Without jitter, the same failure time and same fixed delay produce one concentrated retry wave. Full jitter spreads those retries across the interval in expectation; short subintervals can still be uneven. It changes the concentration of load, not the total number of retries. Attempt and aggregate retry budgets remain necessary.
